items.stem: Study Sources A to C. Source A: a historian writing in 2000 (illustrative). “The road to war ran through Hitler's ideology. Others made mistakes, but only one man wanted to conquer the east and was willing to risk war to do it.” Source B: the Hossbach Memorandum, November 1937 (summary). The record of the meeting states that Hitler told his commanders that Germany's problem of living space could be solved only by force, and that action against Austria and Czechoslovakia might come as early as 1938. Source C: A. J. P. Taylor, The Origins of the Second World War, 1961 (summary of the argument). Taylor argued that Hitler was a traditional German statesman who exploited opportunities created by others, and that the war of 1939 resulted from diplomatic blunders on all sides. How far do Sources A, B and C support the view that Hitler was responsible for the outbreak of war in 1939?
items.answer: Source A supports: it places responsibility on Hitler. Evaluation: it is one interpretation. Source B supports: it shows Hitler intended expansion by force. Evaluation: it was written from memory days later and its status as a "plan" is disputed. Source C challenges: it argues responsibility was shared. Evaluation: his interpretation was controversial and was criticised for ignoring Nazi ideology. Grouping: support A, B; challenge C. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.

items.stem: In 1902 the British economist J. A. Hobson published Imperialism: A Study. ‘Economic motives were the main reason for the new imperialism.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: Industrial powers wanted raw materials such as rubber and palm oil. Businesses sought new markets and investment opportunities. Hobson and Lenin argued finance capital drove expansion. Against: Most investment went to non-colonial areas. Strategic rivalry, such as protecting routes to India, drove many annexations. Nationalism and prestige mattered, especially for Germany and Italy. Men on the spot and missionaries often acted without government approval. Judgement: economic interests were important, but much expansion was strategic and political, driven by rivalry between the powers.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (18-20): sustained analysis of both sides of the question, supported by precise evidence, with a well-substantiated judgement. Level 4 (15-17): developed analysis of both sides; a judgement is reached but is not fully supported. Level 3 (10-14): analysis of one side, or of both with limited development or accuracy. Level 2 (6-9): mainly descriptive, with implicit links to the question. Level 1 (1-5): general assertions with little accurate knowledge. Agree / supporting: Industrial powers wanted raw materials such as rubber and palm oil. Businesses sought new markets and investment opportunities. Hobson and Lenin argued finance capital drove expansion. Disagree / other factors: Most investment went to non-colonial areas. Strategic rivalry, such as protecting routes to India, drove many annexations. Nationalism and prestige mattered, especially for Germany and Italy. Men on the spot and missionaries often acted without government approval. Possible judgement: economic interests were important, but much expansion was strategic and political, driven by rivalry between the powers. [19]

items.stem: Study Sources A and B. Source A: a cahier de doléances of a rural parish, spring 1789 (illustrative). “We pay the taille, the tithe and the dues of the lord, while those who own the most pay least. We ask that all subjects bear taxes equally and that the lord's rights over our harvest be abolished.” Source B: a pamphlet by the Abbé Sieyès, What is the Third Estate?, January 1789 (abridged). “What is the Third Estate? Everything. What has it been until now in the political order? Nothing. What does it ask? To become something.” Compare and contrast the views of Sources A and B on the causes of the French Revolution.
items.answer: Source A: It shows peasants resented unequal taxation and feudal dues. Source B: Sieyès argues that the Third Estate is the real nation but has been excluded from political power. Both challenge the view that the French Revolution was caused mainly by the financial crisis of the monarchy; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: A is a cahier de doléances of a rural parish, spring 1789 (illustrative) (they were often drafted by local lawyers and may not reflect every villager's view); B is a pamphlet by the Abbé Sieyès, What is the Third Estate?, January 1789 (abridged) (it is a piece of political propaganda written to win support). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference. Level 1 (1-3): describes or paraphrases the content of the sources without valid comparison. [15]

items.stem: To what extent did enslaved people free themselves during the Civil War?
items.answer: For: Hundreds of thousands fled to Union lines. Escapes forced Union commanders and Congress to act. Black soldiers fought for the Union. Against: Union armies were needed to make freedom real. The Proclamation and Thirteenth Amendment provided legal freedom. Many enslaved people far from Union lines remained enslaved until 1865. Judgement: enslaved people played a central role in destroying slavery, but their freedom depended on Union victory and federal law.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (18-20): sustained analysis of both sides of the question, supported by precise evidence, with a well-substantiated judgement. Level 4 (15-17): developed analysis of both sides; a judgement is reached but is not fully supported. Level 3 (10-14): analysis of one side, or of both with limited development or accuracy. Level 2 (6-9): mainly descriptive, with implicit links to the question. Level 1 (1-5): general assertions with little accurate knowledge. Agree / supporting: Hundreds of thousands fled to Union lines. Escapes forced Union commanders and Congress to act. Black soldiers fought for the Union. Disagree / other factors: Union armies were needed to make freedom real. The Proclamation and Thirteenth Amendment provided legal freedom. Many enslaved people far from Union lines remained enslaved until 1865. Possible judgement: enslaved people played a central role in destroying slavery, but their freedom depended on Union victory and federal law. [20]

items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [1]

items.stem: ‘Bonaparte came to power in 1799 mainly because of the weakness of the Directory.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: The Directory had no stable majority and overturned elections, so it lacked legitimacy. Corruption and economic problems made it unpopular. Defeats in 1799 created a sense of crisis. Against: Bonaparte's military reputation from Italy and his propaganda made him uniquely popular. Sieyès and other politicians planned the coup and chose Bonaparte. The army's loyalty to Bonaparte made the coup possible when the deputies resisted. Judgement: the Directory's weakness created the opportunity, but Bonaparte's reputation and army support explain why he, rather than Sieyès, emerged as master of France.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (18-20): sustained analysis of both sides of the question, supported by precise evidence, with a well-substantiated judgement. Level 4 (15-17): developed analysis of both sides; a judgement is reached but is not fully supported. Level 3 (10-14): analysis of one side, or of both with limited development or accuracy. Level 2 (6-9): mainly descriptive, with implicit links to the question. Level 1 (1-5): general assertions with little accurate knowledge. Agree / supporting: The Directory had no stable majority and overturned elections, so it lacked legitimacy. Corruption and economic problems made it unpopular. Defeats in 1799 created a sense of crisis. Disagree / other factors: Bonaparte's military reputation from Italy and his propaganda made him uniquely popular. Sieyès and other politicians planned the coup and chose Bonaparte. The army's loyalty to Bonaparte made the coup possible when the deputies resisted. Possible judgement: the Directory's weakness created the opportunity, but Bonaparte's reputation and army support explain why he, rather than Sieyès, emerged as master of France. [18]

items.stem: Read Source B. “We do not ask to touch slavery where it is. We ask only that the free soil won from Mexico shall stay free for free labour.” (A speech by a northern Free Soil congressman, 1848 (illustrative).) Assess the reliability of Source B as evidence about northern attitudes to the new territories.
items.answer: Reliable because it reflects Free Soil arguments of the time. Less reliable because it is a political speech for a new party seeking votes. Cross-reference: It does not show southern views. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [4]

items.stem: Read the sources carefully. Source A: Upton Sinclair, The Jungle, 1906 (summary). The novel described workers falling into vats and diseased meat being sold to the public in the Chicago stockyards. Source B: a speech by a supporter of Wilson, 1914 (illustrative). “In two years this administration has lowered the tariff, given the nation a sound banking system and put real teeth into the laws against monopoly. No president has done more.” How far do Sources A and B support the view that Theodore Roosevelt was the most successful Progressive president?
items.answer: Source A supports: its publication led Roosevelt to support the Meat Inspection Act. Evaluation: it is a novel, written to persuade, and he exaggerated for effect. Source B challenges: it claims Wilson achieved more than Roosevelt. Evaluation: it is a partisan election speech. Grouping: support A; challenge B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [19]

items.stem: Read Source C. “I began at the mill at eight years old. We worked from six in the morning till eight at night, and the overlooker strapped us if we fell asleep.” (Evidence of a mill worker to a parliamentary committee, 1832 (illustrative).) What does Source C reveal about child labour in factories? Use details of the source to support your answer.
items.answer: It suggests children worked very long hours under harsh discipline. Supporting details: for example, “I began at the mill at eight years old”; each detail should be linked to an inference.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each valid inference and 1 mark for each supporting detail from the source [3]

items.stem: Study Sources A and B. Source A: the Charter Oath, 1868 (translated, abridged). “Evil customs of the past shall be broken off and everything based upon the just laws of nature. Knowledge shall be sought throughout the world so as to strengthen the foundations of imperial rule.” Source B: a British newspaper, 1902 (illustrative). “The alliance with Japan secures our position in the Far East. Should Russia fight Japan, she will fight alone.” “Japan's rise as a world power was due mainly to Meiji modernisation.” How far do Sources A and B support this view?
items.answer: Source A supports: it shows modernisation was a deliberate policy. Evaluation: it is a statement of intent, not evidence of what was achieved. Source B challenges: it stresses diplomacy rather than modernisation. Evaluation: it reflects British interests, not Japanese. Grouping: support A; challenge B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [19]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “the government formed by the seceded states in February 1861, with Jefferson Davis as president”.
items.answer: Confederate States of America
items.markingKey: Confederate States of America: the government formed by the seceded states in February 1861, with Jefferson Davis as president. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “the growth of towns and the movement of people from the countryside into them”.
items.answer: Urbanisation
items.markingKey: Urbanisation: the growth of towns and the movement of people from the countryside into them. [1]

items.stem: Which of these statements is accurate?
options: The Compromise of 1877 was a formal treaty approved by Congress.
The Fourteenth Amendment guaranteed equal protection of the laws.
Freed people were given forty acres of land each by Congress.
The Union blockade was completely effective from 1861.
items.answer: The Fourteenth Amendment guaranteed equal protection of the laws.
items.markingKey: It was ratified in 1868. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Source B is the proclamation of the Consuls to the French people, December 1799 (translated). “Citizens, the Revolution is established upon the principles which began it: it is ended.” Study the source. Which statement best describes the message of Source B?
options: The Consuls claim that the principles of 1789 are secure and that the period of revolutionary upheaval is over.
It suggests the crown was close to bankruptcy and that taxing the privileged was the only solution.
It suggests that rebellion and the threat of invasion led revolutionaries to demand harsh measures.
The historian argues that Napoleon preserved equality before the law but destroyed political liberty.
items.answer: The Consuls claim that the principles of 1789 are secure and that the period of revolutionary upheaval is over.
items.markingKey: Only this statement matches the content of Source B. [1]

items.stem: Nadia ends an essay on “How far had the USA become a world power by 1919?” with this conclusion: “By 1919 the USA had the economic power and had shown the military potential of a world power, but it was unwilling to accept the commitments of one.” Explain one piece of evidence that supports this conclusion and one point a critic could make against it.
items.answer: Evidence the conclusion rests on (either strand of the judgement), for example: Largest industrial economy. / Its army was small before 1917. Possible criticism: the conclusion may underplay the point that Overseas empire and the Panama Canal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for relevant supporting evidence and 1 mark for explaining how it supports the judgement; 1 mark for a valid counter-point and 1 mark for developing it [1]

items.stem: Omar is planning an answer to the question: “How far was Prussian economic strength the main reason for German unification?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Omar could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: economic strength gave Prussia the means, but unification was achieved through Bismarck's diplomacy and military victory. Support: The Zollverein tied the German states to Prussia economically. Industrial growth, coal and railways supported a modern army. Challenge: Bismarck's diplomacy isolated each enemy. Military reform and Moltke's leadership won the wars.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “The Smoot-Hawley Tariff reduced US import duties.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Not accurate. It raised them, provoking retaliation and a collapse in world trade.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [1]

items.stem: Study all the sources. Source A: a cartoon in a British magazine, 1923 (description). The cartoon shows a small dove labelled "League of Nations" hiding behind a chair while a burly figure labelled "Italy" stamps on a map of Corfu. Source B: a League of Nations report on refugee work, 1920s (illustrative). “Through the efforts of the High Commissioner, prisoners of war from twenty-six countries have been returned to their homes, and tens of thousands of refugees have been given identity papers.” How far do Sources A and B support the view that the League was successful in the 1920s?
items.answer: Source A challenges: it shows the League failing against a great power. Evaluation: it is satire and simplifies events. Source B supports: it shows the League's humanitarian success. Evaluation: it was written to present the League positively. Grouping: support B; challenge A. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.

items.stem: Study Source D. Source D: Andrew Carnegie, The Gospel of Wealth, 1889 (summary). Carnegie argued that competition was hard on individuals but best for the race, and that the rich should use their surplus wealth during their lifetimes for the good of the community. Assess the reliability of Source D as evidence about the views of industrialists.
items.answer: Reliable because it shows the views of a leading industrialist. Less reliable because Carnegie was defending himself and his class. Cross-reference: It does not show the views of workers. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [3]

items.stem: Read the sources carefully. Source A: a newspaper in a southern state, 1850 (illustrative). “The Union is saved. The South has her Fugitive Slave Law and the North has California. Let agitation now cease.” Source B: a speech by a northern Free Soil congressman, 1848 (illustrative). “We do not ask to touch slavery where it is. We ask only that the free soil won from Mexico shall stay free for free labour.” How far do Sources A and B support the view that the Compromise of 1850 settled the issue of slavery in the territories?
items.answer: Source A supports: it presents the Compromise as ending agitation. Evaluation: a single newspaper may reflect the views of its editor and party. Source B challenges: it shows that northerners would not accept slavery in the new territories, which the Compromise did not resolve. Evaluation: it is a political speech for a new party seeking votes. Grouping: support A; challenge B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [17]

items.stem: Study Sources B and C. Source B: a letter from a magistrate to the Home Office, 1842 (illustrative). “The troops arrived in good time and the meeting dispersed quietly. Since the mills reopened, the Charter is less talked of in the town.” Source C: the People's Charter, 1838 (summary of its six points). The Charter demanded a vote for every man over twenty-one, the secret ballot, no property qualification for MPs, payment of MPs, equal constituencies and annual parliaments. Compare and contrast the views of Sources B and C on political responses to industrialisation.
items.answer: Source B: It suggests troops and economic recovery reduced Chartist activity. Source C: It shows the Chartists demanded democratic political reform. They should be compared on what each says about political responses to industrialisation; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: B is a letter from a magistrate to the Home Office, 1842 (illustrative) (a magistrate had reasons to stress his own success in keeping order); C is the People's Charter, 1838 (summary of its six points) (it shows aims, not how much support or unity the movement had). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference. Level 1 (1-3): describes or paraphrases the content of the sources without valid comparison. [12]

items.stem: Study all the sources. Source A: a speech by a Union general, 1865 (illustrative). “It was not numbers alone. We won when we learned to fight as one army, under one plan, and to strike at the South's railways, crops and will to resist.” Source B: a letter from a Confederate officer, 1864 (illustrative). “We are beaten not by their courage but by their numbers. For every man we lose they bring two, and our men are barefoot while theirs have new boots and full wagons.” How far do Sources A and B support the view that the Union won mainly because of its greater economic resources?
items.answer: Source A challenges: it stresses strategy and leadership rather than resources. Evaluation: he had reasons to emphasise the skill of the generals. Source B supports: it stresses northern numbers and supplies. Evaluation: Confederates had reasons to blame numbers rather than their own failings (the later "Lost Cause" argument). Grouping: support B; challenge A. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [17]

items.stem: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Federal troops supported the strikers in the Pullman strike of 1894.
The transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869.
The Sherman Antitrust Act quickly broke up most trusts in the 1890s.
items.answer: The transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869.
items.markingKey: The lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “The department is calm. The purchasers of national lands are reassured by the Code, the priests preach obedience, and conscription is accepted, if not loved.” (A report by a prefect to the minister of the interior, 1806 (illustrative).) Which statement best describes the message of Source A?
options: Robespierre argues that terror is necessary in a revolution to protect virtue and the Republic.
It suggests that Napoleon's policies brought order and reassured property owners.
Sieyès argues that the Third Estate is the real nation but has been excluded from political power.
It suggests that rebellion and the threat of invasion led revolutionaries to demand harsh measures.
items.answer: It suggests that Napoleon's policies brought order and reassured property owners.
items.markingKey: Only this statement matches the content of Source A. [1]

items.stem: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The Wilmot Proviso became law in 1846.
The Missouri Compromise banned slavery in all western territories.
Virginia seceded after the attack on Fort Sumter.
The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a slave state.
items.answer: Virginia seceded after the attack on Fort Sumter.
items.markingKey: Virginia seceded in April 1861 after Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Mateo is planning an answer to the question: “How far was the Abyssinian crisis more damaging to the League than the Manchurian crisis?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Mateo could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: Manchuria showed the League's weakness, but Abyssinia destroyed its credibility because sanctions were imposed and then undermined by its leading members. Support: Abyssinia was in Europe's sphere and closer to Britain and France, so failure was more obvious. The Hoare-Laval Pact showed members undermining their own League. Challenge: Manchuria set the precedent that aggression would go unpunished. Japan's departure showed great powers could defy the League.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [5]

items.stem: A student writes: “Bismarck said that the great questions of the day would be decided by "iron and blood".” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Accurate. In a speech to the budget committee of the Prussian Landtag in September 1862.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [1]

items.stem: ‘The Spanish-American War marked a turning point in US foreign policy.’ How far do you agree?
items.answer: For: The USA acquired an overseas empire for the first time. It became a Pacific power with the Philippines and Hawaii. It led to more active policies such as the Open Door, the Roosevelt Corollary and the Panama Canal. Against: The USA had already expanded across the continent and bought Alaska in 1867. The Monroe Doctrine had long claimed influence in Latin America. The USA remained reluctant to join alliances and rejected the League in 1919-20. Judgement: it was a turning point in that the USA became an overseas imperial power, but there was continuity in expansionism and in avoiding European alliances.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (18-20): sustained analysis of both sides of the question, supported by precise evidence, with a well-substantiated judgement. Level 4 (15-17): developed analysis of both sides; a judgement is reached but is not fully supported. Level 3 (10-14): analysis of one side, or of both with limited development or accuracy. Level 2 (6-9): mainly descriptive, with implicit links to the question. Level 1 (1-5): general assertions with little accurate knowledge. Agree / supporting: The USA acquired an overseas empire for the first time. It became a Pacific power with the Philippines and Hawaii. It led to more active policies such as the Open Door, the Roosevelt Corollary and the Panama Canal. Disagree / other factors: The USA had already expanded across the continent and bought Alaska in 1867. The Monroe Doctrine had long claimed influence in Latin America. The USA remained reluctant to join alliances and rejected the League in 1919-20. Possible judgement: it was a turning point in that the USA became an overseas imperial power, but there was continuity in expansionism and in avoiding European alliances. [19]

items.stem: Source B is a speech by a French deputy, 1926 (illustrative). “Germany has signed at Locarno. She accepts the Rhine frontier freely. For the first time since the war, France can sleep at night.” Study the source. Why do you think Source B was published? Use details of the source and your knowledge of the context.
items.answer: To welcome Locarno and support Briand's policy. Detail: It suggests Locarno gave France a sense of security.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the purpose; up to 2 marks for explaining it with details of the source; up to 2 marks for setting it in the context of the date [4]

items.stem: To what extent was Reconstruction a failure?
items.answer: For: Black political rights were largely lost by 1900. Freed people did not gain land. Segregation and violence followed. Against: Slavery was abolished permanently. The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments became the basis of later civil rights. Black churches, schools and communities endured. Judgement: Reconstruction failed in its immediate aim of securing equal rights, but it left constitutional foundations that were later used to win them.

Level 2 (6-9): mainly descriptive, with implicit links to the question. Level 1 (1-5): general assertions with little accurate knowledge. The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments became the basis of later civil rights. Black churches, schools and communities endured. Possible judgement: Reconstruction failed in its immediate aim of securing equal rights, but it left constitutional foundations that were later used to win them. [20]

items.stem: Source D is a speech by a Manchester merchant, 1830s (illustrative). “Goods that took a week by canal now reach Liverpool in a day. Our trade has never been so brisk, and every foundry in the district is busy making rails and engines.” Study the source. Does Source D support the view that the railways were the most important economic development of the period? Explain your answer using the source and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Supports: it presents railways as transforming trade and industry However, he is an enthusiast who may exaggerate the benefits.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid judgement; up to 2 marks for details of the source used to support it; up to 2 marks for evaluating the source (provenance or own knowledge) [5]

items.stem: Study Sources A and B. Source A: Upton Sinclair, The Jungle, 1906 (summary). The novel described workers falling into vats and diseased meat being sold to the public in the Chicago stockyards. Source B: a speech by a supporter of Wilson, 1914 (illustrative). “In two years this administration has lowered the tariff, given the nation a sound banking system and put real teeth into the laws against monopoly. No president has done more.” Compare and contrast the views of Sources A and B on Progressive reform.
items.answer: Source A: It exposed unsafe and unhygienic conditions in meat-packing. Source B: It suggests Wilson's reforms were greater than those of earlier presidents. They disagree about whether Theodore Roosevelt was the most successful Progressive president; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: A is Upton Sinclair, The Jungle, 1906 (summary) (it is a novel, written to persuade, and he exaggerated for effect); B is a speech by a supporter of Wilson, 1914 (illustrative) (it is a partisan election speech). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.

Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference.
